title: Under the Island

pages.text:
*The Gatekeeper's Rules, Rule 8: Never go where the water has not been asked.*

The Magpie rocked gently in the harbor, her white hull bobbing against the current that had not yet decided to go anywhere. Shu stood on the gunwale, holding a thick coil of hemp rope that smelled of tar and old rain. She had spent the morning braiding it, testing every knot with a weight that could break a thumb, and now she held it out to Han like a contract.

"Rule one," she said, her voice tight with a seriousness that made her feel taller than she was. "The line is the only thing between you and the bottom. If the line stops, you stop. If the line tugs, you come up. Do you understand?"

Han, perched on the bow with his boots crossed, looked at the rope, then at Shu, and saluted with a hand that had just finished eating a taro ball. "Crystal clear, Captain. I will obey the hemp. It is a very strict gentleman."

"Rule two. Depth. Three meters. No more. The pressure will not care about your curiosity, and neither will I."

"Three meters is a long way to fall," Han said, grinning. "I will count the seconds. One, two, three. If I hit the bottom on the fourth, I will blame the lake for being too eager."

"A-Bao," Shu called out.

The boy appeared from behind a stack of crates, holding his duckling, Dumpling, in a small wicker basket. He looked up with the solemnity of a junior auditor.

"Official Whistle Counter," Shu announced. "If Han goes down, you count the seconds. If the count hits thirty, you blow the whistle. Once. If he is not up in ten more, you blow again. Do not blow for snacks. Do not blow for Dumpling’s opinions. Only for the emergency."

A-Bao took the small brass whistle from Shu’s belt and held it up to the light. "I am very serious about this," he said. "I will not miss a beat."

Shu looked at the water, dark and still as a mirror that had forgotten how to reflect. She looked at Han, who was already adjusting his life vest with the casual confidence of a man who had never once been wrong about water. She took a breath that tasted of salt and fried onions, and then she handed him the end of the rope.

"Go," she said. "And remember. The lake does not hate you. It is just very, very deep."
pages.image: Shu, a sixteen-year-old girl in an indigo jacket and green rain boots, stands on a wooden ferry bow holding a thick hemp rope, while Han, a tall tanned boy in an orange life vest, salutes with a taro ball in hand, and A-Bao, a small boy in a yellow raincoat, holds a brass whistle seriously.

pages.text:
The water was cold in a way that felt personal, as if it had read Han’s name and decided to make him pay for it. He slipped over the side of the Magpie with a splash that was too loud for such a quiet morning, and the cold bit into his skin through the neoprene suit, which was two sizes too large and therefore very good at letting the lake in.

He kicked his legs, finding the rhythm, and let his feet touch the muddy bottom. The silt stirred, rising in a cloud of brown sediment that obscured his view. He adjusted his snorkel, tasting the metallic tang of the air, and looked down.

Shu’s voice came from above, muffled by the water and the distance. "Count, A-Bao."

"One," the boy’s voice sounded, small and far away, like a coin dropped in a well.

Han kept his lungs full. The light filtered down through the green water, turning the world into a murky aquarium. He could see his own hands, blue-tinged and trembling slightly in the cold. He could see the rope, a straight line going up into the brightness, connecting him to the boat, to the sun, to the world of dry boots and warm tea.

"Two," A-Bao counted.

Han pushed off the silt. The water resisted him, thick and heavy, but he swam upward, kicking with steady strokes. He watched the line pay out from the boat above, a taut thread of safety in the green dark. The pressure built in his ears, a dull ache that he knew meant he was deep enough to be interesting.

"Three," A-Bao said.

Han stopped. He hung in the water, suspended between the bottom and the boat, and waited for the fourth count. It did not come. He was not at the bottom yet. He was not at the limit. He turned his head to the left, where the shadow of the island lay thick and heavy, and saw a shape that did not belong in the mud.

It was stone. It was old. And it was looking at him.
pages.image: Han, a tanned boy in a wet neoprene suit and snorkel, swims underwater in murky green water, holding a thick hemp rope that leads up to the surface, with a large, dark stone shape visible in the distance below him.

pages.text:
Han breached the surface with a sharp intake of air that sounded less like a man and more like a kettle reaching its boil. The Magpie shuddered under the sudden weight, rocking hard as he hauled his dripping limbs over the gunwale. Shu caught his arm, her grip steady and cool, while A-Bao stood on the opposite bench, eyes wide, and released his held breath in a long, whistling whoosh.

"What?" Shu asked, leaning forward. Her eyes were sharp. "Is it a fish? A very large fish?"

"No," Han managed. His teeth were chattering so violently that his consonants were turning into slurs. "It is a... a mouth."

Shu looked down at the water. The surface was calm, mirroring the bright sky, but the reflection was broken by a dark shape beneath them. The water here was clear enough that they could both see it without diving.

It was a stone arch, rising from the silt in a perfect, ancient curve. In the center of the arch, half-buried in grey mud, sat a head. It was not a human head. It was carved from grey rock, with long, flowing ridges that suggested a mane and a snout curled back in what looked like a permanent sneer. The eyes were bronze, green with age, and they stared out into the green water with a patience that felt older than the mountain itself.

Spanning the opening was a gate. It was made of wood, bound with strips of bronze that had turned black with rust and time, and it was jammed shut. Packed tight against the stone face of the gate was a dense plug of grey silt. Behind that obstruction, a dark, straight shape lay parallel to the stone. It looked suspiciously like a tree trunk.

"The Dragon," Han whispered. "The Sun Dragon."

Shu reached over and pulled the tether rope, tightening it to stop the boat from drifting further away. "Describe it," she said. Her voice was steady, though her knuckles were white where she gripped the rail. "Every detail. Write it down later. For now, just look."

Han looked. He saw the grain of the wood, the dark bronze bindings, the grey silt, and the trapped log. He saw the way the water flowed around the arch, a slow, respectful current that seemed to bow to the stone. And he felt, for the first time, that the lake was not just water. It was a machine. And it was broken.
pages.image: Underwater view of a large stone arch with a carved dragon head with bronze eyes, half buried in silt, with a wooden gate bound in bronze jammed shut across the opening, and a dark tree trunk visible behind the silt, in murky green water.

pages.text:
"Again," Shu said, before Han could offer to go back. "I’m coming with you this time."

Han blinked, water dripping from his nose. "You? In that suit?"

"I have a mask," Shu said, and pulled a rubber mask from her pocket. It was borrowed from a fisherman who had not noticed it was missing, and it fit her face with a snug, suffocating tightness. She adjusted the strap, feeling the rubber bite into her skin. "If you can see it, I can see it. And I need to see the socket."

They went down together. This time, Shu held the line, and Han guided her to the arch. The water was colder than before, and her breath came in short, sharp puffs through the snorkel. She could see the dragon’s jaw, a long, curved piece of stone that opened into a dark throat. And there, on the side of the arch, was the socket.

It was a vertical slot, cut into the stone, deep and narrow. And in it, a bronze stub. It was not a pin. It was a broken piece, sheared off clean, as if someone had cut it with a sword. The metal was dull, covered in a thin layer of green corrosion, and it looked fragile, like a snapped bamboo stalk left to dry in the sun.

Shu reached out and touched it. The metal was cold, and it vibrated slightly in the current. She felt the solid reality of the years in that small piece of bronze. Thirty years of stillness. Thirty years of water pushing against wood, of silt piling up, of the lake holding its breath.

She pulled her hand back, and her eyes stung. She blinked, and when she opened them, she saw tears running down her cheeks inside the mask. She blamed the lake water. She blamed the cold. She blamed the salt air that had followed them in the boat. She did not blame the feeling that the bronze stub was a wound, and that she had just touched it.

"Three meters," A-Bao’s voice came from above, muffled and urgent. "Time to come up."

Shu nodded, and they kicked upward, rising through the green water, leaving the dragon’s broken pin behind them in the dark.
pages.image: Shu, wearing a rubber diving mask and snorkel, and Han, in a wet neoprene suit, swim underwater near a stone arch, with Shu reaching out to touch a broken bronze pin in a vertical slot on the stone, in murky green water.

pages.text:
The Magpie rocked gently in the harbor, its hull creaking against the pilings, while the dock remained empty save for the lingering scent of frying oil and the distant, rhythmic whine of a scooter engine. Shu and Han climbed onto the wooden planks, their clothes heavy and dripping, and stood there for a moment, catching their breath as their hearts settled. A-Bao stood by the railing, holding his duckling’s basket, his face serious and proud, watching them with an intensity that suggested he had been counting every second of their absence.

They turned, expecting to see Aunt Meng with a plate of scallion pancakes, or Uncle Liu with a mop and a lecture. Instead, they saw A-gong.

He was standing at the very end of the dock, leaning on his bamboo cane, his white hair thin and wispy in the cool breeze. He wore his faded grey vest and his straw hat, and he looked small against the vast, grey sky. He did not look at Shu, nor did he look at Han. He looked only at the water, at the dark, still surface that had just swallowed his granddaughter and his ferry boy.

Shu took a step forward, her wet boots squeaking on the planks. "A-gong," she said, her voice rough. "We saw it. The gate. It’s broken. The pin is sheared."

A-gong did not turn. His hand tightened on the cane, his knuckles white against the bamboo. The silence stretched out, thin and taut, like the rope they had just used to haul themselves up. Then he spoke, his voice low and dry, like leaves scraping across a stone path.

"You went under the island," he said. It was not a question. It was a statement of fact, heavy with a weight that Shu could feel pressing against her ribs.

"We had to," Shu said, her voice trembling slightly. "We had to see it."

A-gong turned away. He walked slowly toward the path that led up to the village, his cane tapping a steady, deliberate rhythm on the wet wood. He did not look back. And then, as he disappeared around the corner of the house, Shu heard him. His voice was quiet, barely a whisper, but it carried clearly over the sound of the waves lapping against the pilings.

"I told them not to ask the lake," he said.

Shu stood on the dock, the salt drying on her skin, and felt the ground shift beneath her feet. Not the ground, she realized. The story. The story had just changed, and she was standing in the middle of it, with the water rising around her.
pages.image: A-gong, an elderly man in a grey vest and straw hat, leans on a bamboo cane at the end of a wooden dock, looking away from the water, while in the foreground Shu and Han stand dripping, watching him, with a misty lake in the background.
